transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Welcome to Deconstructing Yourself, the podcast for metamodern mutants interested in meditation, awakening, vajrayana, tantra, everything Iain M. Banks ever wrote, non-duality, consciousness hacking, and much, much more. My name is Michael Taft, your host on the podcast, and in this episode, I'm speaking with Peter McEwen. Peter McEwen is a meditation coach and founder of The Field, which offers training, community, and the demystification of basic contemplative practices. Peter McEwen has been an ordained Vajrayana yogi since 1993 under the tutelage of Dzongsar Khyentse Rinpoche, Lama Pema Dorje Rinpoche, and Bruce Tift. He has completed the traditional three-year retreat curriculum of Vajrayana Buddhism. And now I give you the episode I call Practicing Tummo with Peter McEwen.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Peter, welcome to the Deconstructing Yourself podcast.

transcript.speaker: Peter McEwen
transcript.text: Pleasure to be here.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, it's a pleasure to have you on the show. After all these years, I was just recollecting that you are the person who designed the logo for Deconstructing Yourself back in something like 2016 or 2017.

transcript.speaker: Peter McEwen
transcript.text: That's right. Yeah, I did. It was a fun little project. I just remember you provided a kind of a picture that was a pastiche of these rust tones that had like a real urban feel to it. And you just said, hey, I want this plugged into some sort of branding for my podcast. And it was such a pleasure to work with such an awesome, easygoing client. Very rare. Did we get in touch, I think, over Twitter, right? I was just like, hey, I'm looking for someone to — I think through Kelly Boyce. And then later on I did some work for Wisdom Labs.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: That's right. I don't know if you are a contractor for them anymore, but I'm pretty sure at the time you were helping them with mindfulness, maybe corporate trainings or something like that.

transcript.speaker: Peter McEwen
transcript.text: Yeah, actually, I was helping them to create a podcast. They worked with Peter before doing logo stuff, so we'll do that again.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Okay, so recently then — so we've known each other in this one capacity for all these years, and I met you in Boulder at least once, maybe several times. But recently I was seeing your posts on Twitter, and I was very happy to discover that you had started publicly teaching tummo. And so I thought, oh, that's really interesting. And I looked at what you were doing and I hadn't known that you were so deeply into it. I knew you were a Dzogchen practitioner and assumed you were doing tummo and the like, but I didn't realize that you were at a stage of many, many, many thousands of hours of practice of this stuff and where you were able to teach it. And so I sent some of my students over there because I was teaching them certain pranayamas, and I thought they might be interested in the Vajrayana, tummo-style stuff. And the rest is all a good story, right? I've been so amazed at what you've put out there and your teaching. And I wanted to bring you on the show here just to talk about it, because as you know, tummo's such a popular topic and sort of what I would consider to be like the supplement bro subculture online or whatever. Lots of kind of macho videos of people jumping into the ice and so on. And so it's out there in a big way. If you put the word tummo into YouTube, you get hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of videos. Most of them don't inspire confidence, at least to me, when I see what they're teaching and how they're teaching it. And so I really wanted to talk to you as someone who knows what they're talking about, about tummo practice and see what you had to say about it.

transcript.speaker: Peter McEwen
transcript.text: That sounds great. I'm happy to talk about tummo, which is just one of the amazing methods that are a component of the Anu Yoga practices within the nine-yana system of the Nyingmapa Vajrayana, and also popularized, of course, in the six yogas of Naropa. The reason I wanted to go public with it — I felt a personal responsibility. I have a little bit of this gadfly DNA in me. And so I was seeing a lot of this YouTube activity, you know, which is natural because of Wim's popularity. You know, he has some really amazing practices of substance that help a lot of people. But he admittedly is not a tummo practitioner, nor is he particularly a proponent of it. But I can see why people would take a practice that is known as being sort of guarded jealously and trying to demonstrate it online through various channels. And in the end, what I saw, I thought maybe was kind of harmful for people to try to, you know, just go sit out in the cold with no clothes on and then practicing incorrect technique. So to some degree, I thought, okay, I'm going to do some public service here and try to draw attention to my understanding of tummo and the tummo practices that were communicated to me by my amazing teachers over the years. So that was the impetus — maybe a little bit of meanness towards taking something I find precious and enjoyable and constructive being commodified and broadcast by people who didn't know what the fuck they're talking about. To me, it's like if you were looking up how to change your brakes on your Honda Civic and they give you the wrong recipe and then your brakes go out, you know, that's not a great way to operate. And I felt a similar feeling about how tummo is being communicated in a popular sense.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, it's dangerous to do it wrong, right? I mean, this is the thing with all pranayama. And even though I'm not a tummo teacher, I teach other forms of like Hindu tantric pranayama, and number one, teaching it wrong, incorrectly, is always going to be a big problem. But furthermore, I mean, even if someone's doing it right, there's a lot of ways that they can accidentally harm themselves if you're not really, really careful. It's always a little startling and upsetting to see what's there on YouTube and what they're recommending doing, because the mood is just so cavalier, and I'm like, you could actually really mess somebody up just recommending that they do that.

transcript.speaker: Peter McEwen
transcript.text: So I think even on a more subtle level — I agree with you 100%. On a material reality level, it is irresponsible to communicate a practice you haven't really gone deep with, in my opinion. That's just my bias. But secondly, you generate confusion for people who are authentically or sincerely interested in learning a method. And when someone's interested in learning something and they learn it the wrong way, it generates a lot of confusion. And maybe then they lose interest in the method. And I would say a lot of the so-called samaya pledges that Vajrayana practitioners make is, you know, not to create harm and not to create undue confusion for their guru or other practitioners, just because it has a downstream effect on not only the practitioner, but the people that they're connected to also. And especially with these practices like Mahamudra, Dzogchen, higher Indic tantras, Anu Yoga — the more you're going for this transcendence or escape from embodied experience, the more confusion is generated, and then it becomes a vicious cycle that can perpetuate itself. So best to start with, you know, positively charged fundamentals and learn it correctly from the ground up. Again, that's just my perspective.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Very good. So let's start with how you got involved with this and learned it from the ground up. What attracted you to learning tummo?

transcript.speaker: Peter McEwen
transcript.text: Well, I'll keep it brief. In 1993, I had a few spontaneous awakenings after my teenage years just being completely panic-ridden. I had really bad panic attacks. It came to the point where even like staying in a classroom was really challenging for me because I thought I was going to have some sort of embarrassing episode. And then when I got away to college, I moved to Santa Barbara and all of a sudden I started having these spontaneous awakenings and had a new reference point. And I think anyone listening to this podcast can probably relate to just the profound impact having a new reference point can have. And then you start doing the work of stabilizing the access to that reference point. And I got really into dharma. Lama Tarchin was teaching. Alan Wallace was a university professor at my college. And eventually I moved to New Zealand with my girlfriend and we were living at a retreat center. And I think these core vulnerabilities always seem to find a way to express themselves through the most inconvenient means. And so when we were over there, you know, everything was so blissful and awesome. You're living in this beautiful Hobbiton kind of environment on a farm and you're doing practice and you're having, you know, great sex perhaps. And then I started having premature ejaculation. And, you know, that's very disturbing for my partner and myself.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Do you think that it was in any way related to the previous panic attacks or the awakenings, or was it utterly separate phenomena?

transcript.speaker: Peter McEwen
transcript.text: I think it is all related to these awakenings. I think, you know, we have awakenings and there's sort of a prompt that there's something more expansive we can attune to. And over time, we tend to collapse back into habitual ways of seeing the world or, you know, imposing formulas on how reality works. And dharma can sometimes provide a convenient formula. The positive aspect of dharma is it has this ability to turn your life upside down when you least expect it. And when we're improperly or maybe unskillfully using dharma, we have this impression, oh, I'm a practitioner, I have the outfit, the beads, I'm saying my mantras. And we're kind of using it as a placeholder for immediate experience. And I think that's because we haven't yet addressed our core vulnerabilities or that sort of core panic that we've constellated our conscious experience around. And I think that core panic, which we also would call open mind, which we do our best to avoid most of the time, it has to find a way to express itself because it's there. It's always there. You can't make it go away. And I think in this case, it's expressed itself through the uncertainty and doubt about my confidence as a lover. So does that sort of answer?

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Oh, absolutely. Yeah, they do seem deeply related. And I was just curious how you were putting that together in your mind.

transcript.speaker: Peter McEwen
transcript.text: I didn't put it together that way when I was 30, which was when it was happening. I'm 51 now. So I could either resist that or I could learn more about my body. So, you know, the Anu Yoga practices — by that point, I had finished ngöndro and qualified, so to speak, to get more access to the tummo practices and working with the subtle body and what we call the completion practice with symbol, Mahamudra with symbol. And I started learning about the energetics of, perhaps within the framework of Vajrayana Buddhism, how these energies coil up and down the spine. And so I kind of came more into consonance with what was actually happening during lovemaking, and working a little bit both at the physiological level with, you know, having a stronger PC muscle, working at the mental level of not collapsing into a sense of low self-worth because I was having this sort of chronic experience of not being able to hold my energies in or satisfy my partner. And then on a more spiritual level, perhaps I was experiencing more openness during lovemaking and more openness in my meditation practice. So this hardship prompted curiosity. And I think that's sort of my understanding of tantric disposition — is a tantric type is a curious person. And yes, we have these really disturbing shocks in our life, and when we recover a little bit of our adult capacity, we start to inquire, why is this happening and what are constructive methods I can use to moderate the suffering that I'm experiencing? So it just happened to be that, for whatever predilection I have, I was really curious about the inner heat yogas.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And so who did you start studying with first?

transcript.speaker: Peter McEwen
transcript.text: Lama Pema Dorje Rinpoche. He was recommended to me by his brother, whose name escapes me right now. I had a mo done, which is a Tibetan divination. And, you know, I was going through a period where I was wondering, who is my root teacher? And the mo returned the tsa lung lama, Lama Pema Dorje Rinpoche. During that period, I was also practicing with Tulku Orgyen and Bhakha Tulku Rinpoche. Both hail from the Pemakö region of northern India. Sort of like a hillbilly Vajrayana, you know, really old school Vajrayana people. But Lama Pema Dorje is a root teacher of mine, and his specialty, his predilection, is the tsa lung style of practice. And last kind of comment on this: I think certain people just have — I don't know a better word than predilection. You know, I think each student has, they're comfortable or find rewarding a certain way of practicing. And that just happens to be something I'm really interested in and fairly confident with.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Good. So when you started working with this, did you immediately find that it was tremendously altering your experience? Once you got involved, what kept you going?

transcript.speaker: Peter McEwen
transcript.text: I think what kept me going is I couldn't make it work. I don't know if you're as hard-headed as I am. Are you, Michael?

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Probably the world's slowest student with this stuff.

transcript.speaker: Peter McEwen
transcript.text: Okay. I am also a slow student. So I've always had to work twice as hard, I feel like, than some of my peers. You know, the reason I kept at it is I just won't give up. You know, when I first started working with breath retention and these postures and being in colder environments with minimal clothing — oh, it was really hard. And it really brought to the forefront my panicked relationship with being embodied, with feeling sensations, working with disturbance. And I found that really interesting. You know, all this time when I was younger, I was practicing a lot. And by this time, I was practicing with another teacher named Dzongsar Khyentse Rinpoche, who's my main teacher. Lama Pema Dorje has since passed. You know, I found the Dzogchen practices to be so much easier, but really what I found in the end is I just found a more reliable way to become disembodied and taking the side of spaciousness, overtaking the side of relative experience. And so to me, a really healthfully oriented practitioner has stopped taking a side with relative experiencing, nor do they take a side with fruitional or open experiencing. They don't really have a bias or preference. But it caught me with my pants down, no pun intended, that I had really started becoming disembodied through these Vajrayana practices. So it was really a great reminder: hey, return to the body. There's some work here to do. Can you sit with a little bit of disturbance and hold your breath for a minute and a half and go through these yogic movements without having, you know, like a nervous breakdown? And it took me, you know, a couple years to get reasonably confident with this method.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So let's dive in there and just quickly describe: what is tummo meditation and what are its origins?

transcript.speaker: Peter McEwen
transcript.text: Well, I think the origins are mysterious. I have never read an account that seemed coherent from a historical perspective. I think each lineage has sort of a mythos about the origins. And usually the mythos has to do with some sort of divine encounter, maybe a treasure teaching or an encounter with a deity that endows the practitioner with the methodology. My bias is that doing tummo or mula bandha — you know, a lot of these inner fire chandali practices hail from India. They're not necessarily Tibetan. And to my mind, they probably were widely used in Mongolia or any other cold place as just a valid method to keep yourself warm in really challenging environments. I'm not a scholar. A lot of people think Niguma, who is purportedly Milarepa's sister, was one of the progenitors of these practices. I'm not sure if anyone really knows. Naropa was Indian, so it's hard to say where he actually got them from. Again, it's all conjectural from my standpoint. And each lineage has a different way of doing it too, which complicates it. The Nyingmapas, the Kagyu, the Gelug, and the Sakyapas all have a different way of engaging with these practices. The tummo practice to me and to Naropa, or the six doctrines of Naropa, is sort of the gateway to working with the vital energies of the body. The other five methods or doctrines — again, it varies by lineage. Certain lineages have eight, certain lineages have six. So these methodologies, which should have the result of not only introduction to the clear light of awareness, but the capacity to absorb oneself into the clear light of awareness — we have a sense that we are independently existent. And so a lot of our resources go into protecting that existence. And so the way that is experienced subjectively is we have stresses, disturbance, we have desires for objects, and a lot of our fascination and fixation is on the objects of awareness. And so these practices ask us to be identified with awareness, not the contents of awareness. And so since we're biological creatures and we probably find that terrifying from the standpoint of our sense of being a significant self, something like tummo is an easy way to kind of massage ourselves into experiencing this luminosity that has no orientation around objects, in a way the ego thinks it's in control of the experience. And the way the ego considers itself in control of the experience of accessing luminosity is through the auspices of breath retention, posture, and visualization at a superficial level. On a more interior level, we're using the winds, the channels which funnel those winds, and these hormonal centers or kundalini centers, also known as chakra or bindu, and we manipulate those in order to maintain connection to our own clear light awareness.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Good, so that's a pretty different description than "we're just going to use our breath to heat ourselves up." Right. And it's certainly the case that when people start to approach an expansive experience of awareness outside the ego or outside the sense of being an individual biological being, the initial response is almost always pure terror, right? It feels like you're dying or being annihilated or whatever. And so what I hear you saying is that tummo can trigger such a response. And in fact, it might be intended to trigger such a response. Is that correct?

transcript.speaker: Peter McEwen
transcript.text: That is my perspective. And I think maybe other people would disagree with that. But to my mind, the breath retention piece will give an incomplete depiction of how the actual practice works. And there's actually scientific evidence that I don't have at hand right now, but I can send over to you at a later date, where the tummo practitioners that are only doing breath retention and posture are unable to increase their core temperature. But the practitioners that have the concentrative skills of holding the visualization and doing the posture and doing the breath retention are able to increase their core temperature. So to some degree, there's some level of concentration that's necessary to make all of this work.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And so this is traditional in lots of pranayamas, but I think, like you're saying, it's left out in most of the, let's say, popularized versions of some form of tummo-esque exercise like Wim Hof and so on. And that is, there's no visualization involved. I'm just curious, for the sake of listeners, can you give a sort of very rudimentary description of how this works, the method by which it works? I mean, just sort of what you're doing when you're doing a tummo practice.

transcript.speaker: Peter McEwen
transcript.text: Yeah, I'll do my best. One caveat about all this is that when you're doing the completion practices, the visualization is a scaffolding that is admittedly constructed. This isn't like perhaps Chinese medicine, where they sort of validate the existence of certain channels and pathways and ways qi flows through the body. We're using a scaffolding and we're creating, so to speak, a new body. And I just want to point out that tummo has a component nested within it that a lot of practitioners are familiar with, and that's the generation practice, where they generate themselves as a deity. And so this is integral to the success of working with tummo, is the ability to generate this sort of holy body, not made of flesh and blood, but made of luminosity. And so the practices of the generation stage, Maha Yoga, is that of replacement. We replace our sense of self-pity, self-absorption, problematic experiencing, with this wholly new way of looking at the world as a deity. And so by the time a tummo practitioner comes into their practice, they probably have some affinity with clear visualization of themselves as a deity. And once you have that, then the breath retention and posture visualization practice takes on a whole new meaning. It requires, you know, some stability in that generation practice.

transcript.speaker: Peter McEwen
transcript.text: So an easy way to do it would be perhaps to visualize yourself as a big luminous bubble. How would that be? And then you would layer into that three main channels — perhaps a blue central channel. Maybe on the right side, you'd have a little thinner channel. And on the left side, you'd have a white channel. And it varies from lineage to lineage. Sometimes the colors are switched up. If it's a dakini practice, perhaps the red channel would be on the left side. So for convenience's sake, let's just say you're a luminous bubble. You have a red right channel, a central channel that's blue, and the left side is white. You inhale through the nose very slowly, very, very slowly. And you fill up these side channels with what we would call errant airs. Perhaps you can call them polluted airs. And these are the airs that create the subject-object dualism. You hold your breath a little longer. You press down with the diaphragm. You pull up with the perineum by contracting the PC muscle. And you create what we call a vase, a little vase there. And then you relax and allow these side airs to be drawn into the central channel by a hot red light, kind of like a spike at the sacrum area. It varies by lineage, but typically it's four finger widths lower from the navel. And you just hold your breath and allow these airs to be absorbed in the central channel, which then arouses, nurtures, supports heat at the central channel. And in that central channel, the heat starts rising upwards, creating a great experience of not only physical warmth at the core — there's also a sense of sensation-level warmth crawling upwards through the spine, or through the central channel in this case.

transcript.speaker: Peter McEwen
transcript.text: And as that warmth crawls upwards, it hits the chakras and melts the bindu or the kundalini that's located at those chakras. Now, the challenge here is, through this habitual clinging to subject and object, this body that I'm describing has become quite crinkled and wound into these sort of unnatural adhesions around this main central channel. And so this warmth straightens out these channels. And when we're initially getting into these practices, it feels almost like we're having to force the air into the central channel. And so a lot of the time in the texts or sadhanas, we are literally talking about forcing the air into the central channel. So that forcefulness we're using, it sort of has this aggression behind it, requires courage. And so tummo means something akin to courageous female. And so this practice in itself of breaking down our fear about not only experiencing bliss, well-being, having a tolerance for intensity, having a tolerance to be nobody, and having a tolerance for clear light awareness — over time we break down our resistances. And those resistances are symbolized or talked about as this crinkling in the energy body.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So you touched on this very briefly, but I want to make sure I'm understanding your view on this, and that is that we're not that concerned with the sort of ontological status of the winds and channels and bindus and so on, correct?

transcript.speaker: Peter McEwen
transcript.text: That's right.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: It's a funny thing that people definitely want to either reject this as non-existent or concretize it as absolutely existent. And neither of those seem to be that helpful of a position about this kind of energy body stuff. Because it's got this interesting quality in that you can't cut someone open and find the energy body. It's not physically there. And yet at the same time, doing these exercises really works, right? Something is happening. And so I find that really, really interesting, because it's like, oh, there's this thing you can do that is really powerful and effective. And it's relying on this — all these visualizations and all this sort of like thousand or maybe thousands of year old understanding of how the human body works, and which may or may not be supported by physiology as we see it today, and yet it really does something. So I just want to hear you talk about that a little further and how you understand it and work with it.

transcript.speaker: Peter McEwen
transcript.text: Yeah, I mean, I think it's a mindset. And from a third person objective view, there's a neurological aspect that supports the notion that a mindset actually improves one's ability to attain an intention. And so if we wanted to use that sort of language, we could say that the Anu Yoga body or the completion body, the vajra body, is a mindset. And so we'll continually find justification probably to use that method because we're looking for some sort of result, some sort of evidence to support its existence. As for the aspect of the subtle body being something that exists independently — that's the beauty of the system. That's the beauty of the methods of Buddhism in general, right? They all have a placebo quality. And so the more we try to reify them as being actually existent, the more we're chasing our own tail. And so the escape hatch for Buddhism to operate properly within the completion practices — yeah, the vajra body or this energetic body is there, but it's not there, right? It's there when you're experiencing it or when you're actually visualizing it. And where does it go when you're not? And you could say that about any of our created states of mind, whether that's depression or whether that's adulation or whether that's a sense of self-confidence and workability. Those are created states arising within a broader context of open awareness.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: I think another thing that points to this in a really fun way is if you look at the history of, in India, the chakra systems and all the nadis and all that — there's many, many, many different systems. It's not like we see today where it's sort of settled on a template of seven chakras and their rainbow colors. The rainbow color is not the way the original system works. But also, in many systems, there's only three chakras, or sometimes there's, I don't know, 14 or 18 chakras, and the way the channels are visualized is different. And I think you indicated it's something similar in Vajrayana, where different systems see it all differently. And so that's a strong indication that part of it is constructed, it's imaginal. And yet, at the same time, it's not nothing, right? In the West, when we hear something's imaginal, that to us means it doesn't exist. Right. This has pretty strong effects for something that doesn't exist.

transcript.speaker: Peter McEwen
transcript.text: Yeah. And I think something like gratitude, which is just maybe some neural activity, right? It ends up having material effects on a person's quality of life. Something as simple as Rick Hanson's admonition to take in the good and really allow that good to penetrate and rewire the brain. It is initially revealed as maybe sensation level experience, like feeling good, and then perhaps it has some sort of neurological qualia, and then it is enacted in our lives. And you could similarly say something about these so-called advanced practices. These methods have a sensation level or radically interior experience. And then probably they're having some sort of neurological change in the brain. And then hopefully that is enacted out in consensus reality, which is mostly just made up of relationships. And so to my mind, the real heart of this practice is being in the body, having your cell phone off for the 30 minutes you're doing the practice, feeling the sensations, familiarizing yourself with your capabilities for visualization, emotional regulation, the ability to stay with disturbing experience without falling into a formula, and having a little devotion to your own potentiality. I think that to me is the most powerful part of this experience for the average practitioner. If you get to the point where your death reenactment practice becomes very formidable and strong and you're able to dissolve into clear light at the heart center — hey, that's wonderful. That's going to probably over time conquer even more subtle fears of death or annihilation.

transcript.speaker: Peter McEwen
transcript.text: But at a more practical level, the way I teach this practice is less focused on some sort of cessation or transcendent function and more about, hey, can you manage your life? Can you manage the ability to have the discipline to practice every day and sit still with disturbance without basically freaking out? And I think those are good qualities for any meditation practitioner, or even anyone who's interested in therapeutic modalities, who maybe are having a harder time with having self-discipline or with enduring intensity without falling into a reactive state. So that's an application I think that's really valuable for anybody. And that's why I chose to publicly teach these, because I think, you know, they have a deeper potential probably to expose us to fundamental open awareness without any hope of resolution or reifying a significant self, but also practically it's leveraging neuroplasticity, breath retention, cold exposure. It's good for the immune system, and it just has all these really helpful byproducts that are generally helpful from what I've seen.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: For you, just personally, having done this for 20 years or so, what have you seen as some of the, let's say, unexpected helpful byproducts of doing tummo?

transcript.speaker: Peter McEwen
transcript.text: I would say my reactivity has been diminished. I would say there's a feeling of lightness or transparency physiologically. It's almost as though the sensations that arise are feather light. The sense of heaviness that sort of was the earmark of my young experience has been moderated to a great degree. A sense of mental clarity — my visualization is formidable and my concentrative skills are formidable. But again, I want to come back to: so much of the things we regret in life, we're having, you know, a reactive episode and we look back on it and we may say to ourselves, oh, the feelings I was having were so vivid and disturbing and scary. And in order to get out of that sense of vulnerability, I reacted in a way that was harmful or hurtful. And I would say the tummo practice for me has helped me moderate my reactions and realize, yeah, this is just a feeling. Maybe it appears like I'm going to be annihilated if I feel this way, but I probably won't be. And then it gives me, most of the time, not all the time, but it gives me pause before I react in a hurtful way. So I think that's the main or the fulcrumatic positive. And then on a more spiritual perspective, if we want to use that word...

transcript.speaker: Peter McEwen
transcript.text: Access to open awareness, basically, by choice. You know, I think when we're younger and we first start having our experiences of openness, it can be so catastrophic to our worldview. And when I was young and I had no control over these experiences of openness, it just shattered my worldview and I was kind of rendered incompetent to operate in consensus reality. It took me a few years to pull it together. But I would say as you iteratively get used to open experience and luminosity, it becomes less of a grand affair or something to get fascinated with. And it just becomes a natural component of everyday life.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: That's beautiful. On a curiosity level, are there any even more mundane side effects, like you're just able to heat your body up more easily, or...?

transcript.speaker: Peter McEwen
transcript.text: Oh, yeah, I forgot about that. Yeah, I mean, I'm so used to it. I live in Boulder, Colorado, and it gets below zero, and I can go out and it'll be below 10 or something and I feel warm. It feels great. It feels like summertime and you just got out of a cold shower. It has that really pleasurable physical byproduct of doing this practice. Also from a more primitive orientation, being able to re-channel ejaculate and have multiple orgasms — that's certainly attractive. That's been well promoted in the West, I realize that. And that's why I don't really play it up too often, but that is a byproduct also, of being able to re-channel, have multiple orgasms.
